name: Ivan Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the rehab ward at the small hospital in my town, mostly older people getting back on their feet after a fall or a stroke. Early shifts start at seven: washes, getting people up and dressed, breakfast, meds, then helping the physios with walking practice. Afternoons it's paperwork, family phone calls and the never-ending fluid charts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the getting-better part. A woman came in last month who couldn't stand, and last week she walked to the day room with a frame and her grandson filmed it. What wears me out is the computer side, honestly, and being the one the sister has to remind about the care plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. I'm not really one for all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd just say good, nothing changes, let's get on with it. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not online much. With my mates at football I'd probably say the robots still can't take a penalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix my problems. Nothing changing sounds nice until you remember nothing was fine to start with. I've had three weeks of money saved since I qualified. Dana works the checkout at the supermarket, and between us we just about cover rent, the car and the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and stop putting off my care plan training. I'd also stop the takeaway on Fridays, because we keep saying we'll save and never do. And I'd keep asking for overtime on the weekends when it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not scared, just aware there's no room if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no room if anything goes wrong. What's gone wrong before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car failed its test in the spring and needed four hundred of work. We put it on the credit card and we're still paying it off. My brother offered to help, but I didn't want to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a bit of extra money if overtime came through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear the card first. Then maybe put a hundred aside in a pot I can't touch. Dana's better at that than me.

say: Good, **nothing changes**, so let's just get on with it.
I'd joke at **football** that robots still can't take a penalty.
think: I'm **relieved**, but nothing was fine to begin with.
Dana's **checkout wage** and mine barely cover rent, car and bills.
do: Stop putting off my **care plan training** on the rehab ward.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** to start saving.
Ask for **weekend overtime** whenever it's offered.
feel: **Flat** rather than scared, aware there is **no room** for mistakes.
S0.quote: Nothing changing sounds nice until you remember nothing was fine to start with. I've had three weeks of money saved since I qualified.
fieldNote: He avoids **computers** and is behind on care plan training.
A **four-hundred** car bill is still on the credit card.
He won't ask his **brother** for help, out of pride.

steps.text: Finish the overdue care plan training on the rehab ward
Stop the Friday takeaway and clear the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That sounds like something they'd actually do to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that nurses do hands-on work, so leave us alone and fix the staffing. With friends I'd say it's the supermarkets you should be worried about, not hospitals. I'd keep it short, I don't like arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the computer side of my job is the part I'm worst at, and it's the part that changes. If they bring in some new AI system for care plans, I'll be the slowest on the ward again. I can get a ninety-year-old man from bed to chair without hurting him. I can't get the new tablet to save my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the hospital actually brings in before doing anything. I'd ask Dana to look at moving off the checkout to the stockroom or the bakery counter. And we'd really start saving, maybe fifty a month, even if it means no holiday this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, if I'm honest. Not for nursing, for Dana and for our money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dana say if you asked her to move off the checkout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say the bakery starts at five in the morning and she's not doing that. She'd be right, too. But the self-checkouts have already taken half the tills, and in this picture they'd take the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the new system arrived, who would you ask for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemal, the other junior on the ward, is good with it. I'd ask him on a quiet night shift when nobody's watching. I don't want the sister to see me struggling again.

say: Nurses do **hands-on work**, so fix **staffing** instead.
It's the **supermarkets** that should be worried about this, not the hospitals.
think: The **computer side** is my weakest part, and it's the part that changes.
Dana's **checkout job** is the real risk for us.
do: **Wait and see** what the hospital brings in before acting.
Ask Dana to look at the **stockroom** or bakery instead of the checkout.
Save **fifty a month**, skipping this year's holiday.
feel: **Worried**, not about nursing, but about Dana and **money**.
S1.quote: I can get a ninety-year-old man from bed to chair without hurting him. I can't get the new tablet to save my notes.
fieldNote: He's **proud** of his hands-on skill and embarrassed by screens.
He'd ask a colleague for help **quietly**, to avoid being seen struggling.
His household's weak spot is Dana's **supermarket checkout** job.

steps.text: Wait to see which care plan system the hospital brings in
Save fifty a month and skip this year's holiday
Help Dana ask about moving to the supermarket stockroom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That's too fast for anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say whoever's in charge, government or the hospital bosses, had better have a plan, because nobody I know does. I'd say it at work and at football. I'm not a protest person, but I'd sign whatever petition came round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it goes in order. My girlfriend's checkout goes first, then the paperwork side of my job, then the lifting. On my pay, the first one is enough to sink us. Then I've got until about 2031 before a robot can lift a patient, and I'm junior, so I'm not the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: sell the car and bike to the hospital, cancel the phone contracts and go to cheap ones. I'd ask my brother if we could stay in his spare room if Dana lost her job. And I'd do every overtime shift going for two years to build some kind of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. The kind where you lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't ask your brother before. Would you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's that or the street, yes. I'd hate it, but I'd ask. My brother's got a house with a box room full of junk, so there's space if we clear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn any of the new AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they made me. I know that's probably stupid. I just think by the time I've learned one, it'll have changed again.

say: Whoever's in charge had better have a **plan**, because nobody I know does.
I'd sign any **petition** going, though I'm not a protester.
think: Dana's **checkout** goes first, then my **paperwork**, then the lifting.
As a **junior**, I wouldn't be kept once robots can lift patients.
do: **Sell the car** and cycle to the hospital to cut costs.
Ask my brother about his **spare room** if Dana loses her job.
Work every **overtime shift** for two years to build a cushion.
S2.quote: My girlfriend's checkout goes first, then the paperwork side of my job, then the lifting. On my pay, the first one is enough to sink us.
fieldNote: He sees the hit coming in a clear **order**: Dana's job, paperwork, lifting.
He'd swallow his **pride** and ask his brother for help.
He still **refuses** to learn AI tools unless forced.

steps.text: Sell the car and cycle to the hospital each day
Clear his brother's box room as a fallback home
Work every weekend overtime shift for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for the government and the hospitals to sort out training and a safety net, so they'd better start. At work I'd say the rehab ward still needs people. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-two when the thinking AI arrives and thirty-five when the robots come. That's time to get properly good at the hands-on side. I'm not a computer person, and five years won't make me one. Five years might make me a better nurse, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my competencies and ask to go on the moving and handling trainer course, because that's hands-on and people trust you. We'd save a little each month, and Dana would look at a care assistant course, since that's harder to automate than a till. I'd learn the computer stuff only as much as I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not lying-awake worried. More like a bill I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the moving and handling trainer course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm actually good at it, and it's teaching people to lift safely. Even when robots come, someone has to teach staff to work next to them. It's the one thing on the ward I'm better at than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dana think about becoming a care assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's good with old people, she does my nan's shopping every week. She'd moan about the pay, but it's not much worse than the checkout. We'd talk about it properly over the weekend.

say: There's **time** to sort out **training** and a safety net, so start now.
think: Five years gives me time to get good at the **hands-on side**.
I won't become a **computer person**, but I could become a better nurse.
do: Apply for the **moving and handling** trainer course.
Help Dana look at a **care assistant** course instead of the till.
Learn the **computer side** only as much as required.
feel: **Worried** but not sleepless, like a **bill** he knows is coming.
S3.quote: I'm not a computer person, and five years won't make me one. Five years might make me a better nurse, though.
fieldNote: He plays to his **strength**: lifting and teaching others to lift.
He sees Dana moving into **care work** as safer than the till.
He's still **minimal** about computers, even with five years.

steps.text: Apply for the moving and handling trainer course
Help Dana look into a care assistant course
Put a small amount aside every month in a separate pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. A lot of things can happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so nobody needs to panic. I'd say the same at work and at home. I'd probably joke that I'll be the old guy telling the robots how we used to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd mostly put it out of my mind. I'd be thirty-seven when the AI comes and forty with the robots. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably just get on with it and deal with the robots when I see one on the ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, get my competencies done, and go for the handling trainer course in a few years. We'd try to save a bit, but honestly we'd probably not change much. I'd let the computer stuff come to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. The money's still tight, and I'm not good at planning ten years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're not good at planning ten years ahead. What about one year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One year I can do. Pay off the card, keep the car going, maybe a week by the sea with Dana. That's about as far as I plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw someone on the ward lose their job because of it. Then it'd feel real. Until then it's just talk on the news.

say: There's **plenty of time**, so nobody needs to **panic**.
I'd joke about telling the **robots** how we used to do it.
think: I'd mostly put it **out of my mind** for now.
I'd deal with **robots** when I see one on the ward.
do: Carry on and finish my **competencies** on the rehab ward.
Go for the **handling trainer** course in a few years.
Pay off the **credit card** and keep the car going.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, because **money** is still tight.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably just get on with it and deal with the robots when I see one on the ward.
fieldNote: He plans **one year** ahead, not ten.
He'd only move faster if he saw a colleague **lose a job**.
His real pressure stays **money**, not AI.

steps.text: Finish his rehab ward competencies this year
Wait until colleagues are affected before learning new systems
Pay off the credit card from the car repair

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Dana and I would both be in trouble at once and there's no money to fall back on. What would help is the hospital giving us proper paid training time, and some kind of help for people like Dana who lose their jobs. Not a lecture, actual money while you retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't good with computers. I'm not against the future. I just want somebody to tell me how I pay the rent while it's arriving. I'll learn what I have to, I just learn it slower.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the future. I just want somebody to tell me how I pay the rent while it's arriving.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a small-town **rehab ward**, strong at lifting and weak at screens.
He lives with Dana, a **supermarket cashier**, with three weeks saved and a credit card debt.
He avoids **AI tools** and would rather wait and see.
He's **uneasy** in the calm pictures and **alarmed** at two years, mostly for Dana.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Dana would both lose income at once.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training time** at the hospital and **money** for people retraining, like Dana.
